extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, associate editors, peer reviewers, and researchers interested in peer-review policy and reform
extracted.subtask_description: Discussion of standards, practices, and proposed reforms to improve the journal peer-review process (e.g., blind reviewing, reviewer accountability, training, rating forms, empirical testing). Aimed at shaping editorial policy and reviewer practices across scientific journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial accountability and responsibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The role of a responsible editor is critical to the peer-review process; editorial accountability and responsibility are essential concepts to endorse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors are central to peer review — they select reviewers, make final determinations, and are expected to be accountable. The text notes nearly all commentators (many of whom are editors) emphasize editorial accountability. Problems cited include editors refusing requests for information and failing to honor confidentiality. Improving peer review implies strengthening editors' responsibilities and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Blind reviewing (single/double blind)
rubrics_metrics.description: Moving to blind reviewing is proposed to remedy numerous concerns and is seen by many commentators as 'a step in the right direction.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence cited (Rosenblatt & Kirk; partial study data) suggests blind reviewing is 'fairly blind' — only 15–30% of reviewers accurately guessed an author's identity and with low confidence. Practical difficulties include authors revealing identity subtly and editors remaining unblinded and making determinations in doubtful cases. Some disciplines (e.g., physics) or reviewers believe author name and institutional identity are important information for reviewers. Consider field differences when implementing blind review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Awareness of institutional-affiliation bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Institutional affiliations may influence reviewers; some view affiliations as reflecting ability, others argue affiliation is not a valid reflection of ability and can introduce bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document reports disagreement: some commentators (e.g., Lazarus) treat affiliation as indicative of ability; others (e.g., Palermo, Tax & Rubinstein) note qualified scientists work at low-prestige institutions. Experimental evidence (e.g., manuscripts submitted with different affiliations) suggests affiliation can affect outcomes. Policy should account for potential 'known' vs 'unknown' institutional bias and consider mechanisms to mitigate it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Different standards for grant versus journal review
rubrics_metrics.description: Blind reviewing may be inappropriate for grant-proposal reviews because reviewers need the PI's background, track record, and institutional resources to assess the likelihood a 'promise' can be fulfilled.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commentators argue grant review requires knowledge of PI identity; however empirical examples (Stark-Adamec & Adamec; Cole et al.) raise concerns about bias and low reliability in grant peer review. Recommendation: weigh the value of PI-identifying information against documented bias; avoid blanket prescriptions without empirical testing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer accountability vs anonymity (open review)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proposals for open review (reviewers' identities made known to authors) are controversial; many argue anonymity protects junior reviewers and prevents retaliation, while others argue anonymity produces unaccountable behavior.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most commentators caution against open review due to protection of less powerful reviewers and potential compromise of review effectiveness. Freese argues against anonymous reviewing, noting anonymous referees have one-sided power and are accountable only to editors. Consider trade-offs: anonymity can reduce retribution risk but may reduce reviewer accountability; alternatives (see paying/acknowledging reviewers) are discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Incentives and recognition for reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: To improve accountability and reduce insulting or ad hominem reviews, suggestions include paying reviewers or acknowledging their names (e.g., adding them to articles they recommended).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proposed interventions: monetary payment, formal acknowledgement, or credit for reviewing activity. These aim to increase reviewer responsibility and reduce low-quality or abusive reviews. Practical and cultural implications (costs, willingness to sign reviews) must be weighed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author's review (author feedback on reviewers)
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'author's review' (a mechanism for authors to review reviewers) was proposed and found to have merit by some commentators but problems by others.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The idea can increase accountability but raises concerns (e.g., potential for retaliation, bias in author evaluations). The text notes mixed reactions; careful design and safeguards would be required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewer training
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewer training is an area examined by recent studies and is presented as a potential way to improve peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Studies (Whitehurst; Cicchetti & Eron) have examined reviewer training. Training could standardize expectations, improve reliability, and reduce inappropriate comments. Implementation should be tested empirically for efficacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of standard rating forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of standard rating forms for reviewers is a suggested procedural reform to improve review quality and reliability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard rating forms can structure evaluations, clarify criteria, and potentially improve interrater reliability. The document cites studies that examined their use; adoption should be piloted and empirically evaluated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interrater reliability and reviewer agreement
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns about lack of reviewer agreement and poor reliability (unsatisfactory reliabilities reported) are central critiques of the peer-review system.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reliability metrics (e.g., intraclass correlation, kappa) and replication studies are needed to quantify reviewer agreement. Recognize that low reliability undermines confidence in decisions; reforms should aim to increase agreement or manage variability (e.g., more reviewers, clearer criteria, structured forms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Empirical testing of reform proposals
rubrics_metrics.description: Suggestions for improvements to peer review need to be tested empirically to assess their impact rather than dismissed as 'it won't work' without evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The authors argue that criticisms claiming reforms 'won't work' often lack empirical basis. Recommended approach: design experiments or observational studies (e.g., trials of blind review, training, rating forms) to measure effects on bias, reliability, and fairness before broad implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-disciplinary comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-disciplinary comparisons are a promising but under-researched area to understand how peer review operates differently across fields.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document suggests differences (e.g., physics vs psychology) may influence attitudes and effects of reforms; comparative research could reveal discipline-specific practices and inform tailored reforms rather than one-size-fits-all policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fairness doctrine (merit-based judgment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Science must uphold a fairness doctrine: everyone should have fair access to journal space and federal funds, judged on the merit of ideas rather than on academic rank, sex, place of work, publication record, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy and practice should ensure decisions are based on intellectual merit and not demographic or institutional attributes. This principle underlies many recommendations (blind review, mitigation of affiliation bias, empirical evaluation of procedures) and is presented as an ethical standard for peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial transparency/cooperation with investigations
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors' cooperation and transparency (e.g., providing original reviewers' comments, describing how detections came about) are necessary for credible assessment and study of peer review practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The notes report that several editors refused requests for additional information and, in one case, breached confidentiality. For studies and reform efforts to proceed, editors should be willing to share information under appropriate safeguards to allow evaluation of review processes.
